CHAIR ( Senator Grogan ): I declare open this hearing of the Senate Finance and Public Administration Legislation Committee into the 2025-26 supplementary budget estimates. I'd like to acknowledge the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present. The committee has set Thursday 6 November 2025 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and Friday 28 November 2025 as the date for return of answers to questions taken on notice. We've not adjusted those from the dates from Friday. If anyone has an issue with that, I'm happy to look at that, but we go on to subsequent estimates hearings in December.

The committee proceedings today will consist of the Department of Parliamentary Services and the Parliamentary Service Commissioner, as listed on the program. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, including answers to questions on notice. I remind witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It's unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at estimates hearings as any questions going to the operations or financial position of departments and agencies which are seeking funds at estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of the hearing. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of the department of the Commonwealth should not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and should be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to a superior officer or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when or how policies were adopted.

Witnesses are reminded that the Senate orders specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I welcome the President, the Hon. Sue Lines; and Ms Jaala Hinchcliffe, the secretary; and other officers of the Department of Parliamentary Services. I also welcome Dr Banerjee, Acting Parliamentary Services Commissioner, and other officers from his department. President, would you care to make an opening statement?

The President: Yes, thank you. Before the Department of Parliamentary Services officials and I answer your questions today I'd like to make a brief statement. This committee has heard evidence from departmental officials in relation to Dr Fiona Roughley's independent investigation into the incentive-to-retire payment provided to a former deputy secretary and the related investigation being conducted by the National Anti-Corruption Commission.

The committee has also had evidence as to the data search that was required to aid these investigations. Alongside original questioning from the Speaker and I in our roles as presiding officers, I do note the concerns of this committee and our parliamentary colleagues in relation to the storage of parliamentary data. I reassure parliamentarians that the Speaker and I take our responsibility to the parliament seriously. I can assure parliamentarians that we believe this data was handled appropriately to aid the independent investigation and the related National Anti-Corruption Commission investigation. The Speaker and I have now formally requested that this data be returned to the Australian parliament. Further, we have requested that DPS and the clerks agree on a procedure for the return, handling and storage of this data within the parliament. We have requested this procedure is approved by the presiding officers before any further action is taken, and I table the letter. Thank you, Chair.

CHAIR: Thank you, President. Ms Hinchcliffe, would you like to make an opening statement?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Good afternoon, Chair and members of the committee. Earlier this afternoon, I provided a letter to the committee containing information on data searches authorised or undertaken by the department to assist in the fact-finding investigation undertaken by Dr Fiona Roughley SC about an incentive-to-retire payment made to a former deputy secretary.

In that letter, I also provided the answers that I could to three questions taken on notice during the committee's hearing last Friday about the data searches authorised or undertaken to support Dr Roughley's investigation. In my letter, I noted that I had sought advice from the National Anti-Corruption Commission about whether the search terms provided to support Dr Roughley's investigation could be disclosed by the committee.

Subsequent to the dispatch of my letter, the NACC has advised that it is of the view that the disclosure by DPS of some of the search terms used to identify data relevant to Dr Roughley's fact-finding investigation would not prejudice the NACC investigation, provided that it was also made clear to the committee that the terms used are relevant to Dr Roughley's investigation and not to the related NACC investigation.

The NACC has further advised that it would be concerned if the names of DPS employees—with the exception of the then secretary and the then deputy secretary—were included in the search terms disclosed to the committee, as this may prejudice its investigation. Accordingly, I provide the following document, which sets out the search terms provided to DPS ICT on 21 June 2024 and 22 August 2024. The search terms that identify DPS employees, other than the then secretary and the then deputy secretary and an APS employee, are not included.

I and the senior executives of the department are now available to answer any questions. I will table that statement and the attached document.

CHAIR: Thank you. I note that we have published various pieces of correspondence that have come in since we last met on Friday. For complete transparency, they are all available. We will publish the further material that you have just provided us with. Dr Banerjee, do you have an opening statement?

Dr Banerjee : No, thank you.

Senator McGRATH: I appreciate everybody coming along this evening. At the crux of this, I would like to remind everybody that this is to do with the protection of parliamentary privilege.

Secretary, I have your letter here with today's date. There were a number of questions from the coalition in relation to the supply of information to the law firm and to their contractor. I do note your advice in there, but at this particular point in time we are not concerned about the information that was supplied to Dr Roughley; it is information supplied to the law firm and to their subcontractor.

There has been some media reporting that the ICT team within DPS had concerns about the provision of emails to the lawyers and their IT contractor, because they were outside the APH system. You sort of touched on this in your letter. Is that correct?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I was provided with a draft risk assessment by the ICT team on, I think, 4 September. Then I had a conversation with the former chief information officer on 5 September about the contents of that draft risk assessment. The draft risk assessment went to both the removal of data from the APH system and also went to the security of HWLE, given their previous data breach. I had discussions with the former chief information officer about the proposed data extraction—the data extraction that I had authorised on 22 August—which was a bulk data extraction from several DPS employee's mailboxes to then be taken offsite to be searched. We agreed that we would split that into two parts: that there were some DPS employee's data that could be extracted in bulk for it to be then searched outside of the system, and that DPS ICT would then conduct searches on the other DPS employees.

Senator McGRATH: You say it is a draft risk assessment?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The risk assessment was in draft; that's right.

Senator McGRATH: Was it called a draft risk assessment?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Yes, it was called draft.

Senator McGRATH: Was it emailed to you?

Ms Hinchcliffe : It was emailed to me, yes.

Senator McGRATH: What is the process for the risk assessments? Is normally a draft prepared and then sent to the senior officer for discussion? So it's a working document? Could you take me through that process.

Ms Hinchcliffe : In this case, a draft was sent to me for discussion, and we had that discussion the next day. I left that meeting with the understanding that the then chief information officer and I were both in agreement that the discussion that we had had and the changes that we had made—in terms of DPS ICT undertaking searches in relation to some of the DPS employees—met the concerns that were raised. I was not provided, at any stage, with a final risk assessment, either one in relation to those concerns or one that had been changed to reflect the changes in approach that we had taken.

Senator McGRATH: Do you have a copy of the draft risk assessment that could be tabled?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Can I take it on notice to provide that for you?

Senator McGRATH: Okay. What did it say the risk assessment was? Does it say 'hot', 'cold'—in terms of the terminology?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The risk assessment, like a normal risk assessment, refers to the risk rating that is given to various actions, in effect. So on a normal risk assessment you would have risk ratings from low, moderate, severe. You would usually have some colouring around that as well—low being green. I think usually moderate is yellow, and severe is normally red.

Senator McGRATH: What was the draft risk assessment?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The draft risk assessment was red. So there were concerns being raised with me.

Senator McGRATH: And those concerns went to the release of information to the lawyers and to the subcontractors?

Ms Hinchcliffe : It went to the bulk extraction of data. Material had by this stage already been released, and it had been released by the DPS ICT staff without any concerns being raised with me through a draft risk assessment or another means about those risks. This was particularly in relation to the second search that I authorised. Because there were serious concerns about first search, the second search was about there being a being a bulk extraction of DPS employee data, for that to be then searched by TransPerfect and provided through a secure mechanism to HWLE to ensure that there was no parliamentary data, and to then be provided to Dr Roughley. This risk assessment was in relation to that, and, as I said, the agreement we came to was that some DPS employee data would be provided on bulk extraction and some would be searched by DPS ICT.

Senator McGRATH: Was there a full extraction?

Ms Hinchcliffe : For some DPS employees, yes, but for some DPS employees the searches were conducted by ICT. I now know that, actually, searches were not just done in relation to those DPS employees. Some searches were conducted across the APH network, which was entirely inappropriate.

Senator McGRATH: In terms of the full mailbox extraction, how many DPS employees had their full mailboxes extracted?

Ms Hinchcliffe : It was two. It was across a date range, as well. I think I put the date ranges in the letter that I sent to you. I think it was 1 February 2023 to 30 November 2023.

Senator McGRATH: Were any protocols put in place to ensure that emails from parliamentarians that were in those mailboxes were isolated?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The protocols that were put in place related to, firstly, that the search terms that were used were search terms that went to the ITR rather than to the broader functioning of parliament. Then there was a process that the data was provided across a system called Relativity, which is a secure system, to be able to provide search results to HWLE. HWLE did not download that data onto their system. It stayed on Relativity, and they then reviewed the results to make sure that there was no parliamentary data within those results.

Senator McGRATH: How would you define 'parliamentary data'? Is an email from Senator.McGrath@aph.gov.au to the departmental secretary—that could cover issues in relation to parliamentary privilege. Can you give a guarantee that emails from parliamentarians did not leave the building?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I can't give you the guarantee that emails from parliamentarians did not leave the building—I was quite clear about that at the hearing last week—because it was a bulk extraction. Yes, if it were in a DPS mailbox that was extracted over that period of time, then it would have left the building and it would be held securely by TransPerfect. But—

Senator McGRATH: Isn't that the issue, though, that data or emails—whatever you want to call them—information that could be covered by parliamentary privilege has left the building in an authorised process run by DPS?

Ms Hinchcliffe : That's the reason why, as I understand it, the presiding officers have now requested that that data be returned to APH, and I will be implementing their direction to me.

Senator McGRATH: How many emails were in the bulk extraction?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I can't provide you with the number of emails, but I can provide you with the amount of data, which is what I provided you in the letter.

Senator McGRATH: I thought I'd asked for that one on notice on Friday—the number of emails.

Ms Hinchcliffe : I don't have the number of emails, but I have got the amount of data. I can continue to see whether I can provide the number of emails, but I can provide you with the amount of data.

CHAIR: When you're ready, Senator McGrath, we'll rotate the call.

Senator McGRATH: I just want to confirm which full inboxes went. It was the former secretary's and the former deputy secretary's?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I need to just be a little bit careful here, so please excuse me while I just take a moment. Yes, I can confirm in terms of an extraction in relation to the former secretary and former deputy secretary, but, for the other DPS employees where the extraction was taken, the NACC have indicated to me that it would prejudice their investigation if I indicated who they were.

Senator McGRATH: Let's take the names out of it. A couple of very senior officers had their full inboxes gone, and other senior officers have had partial extracts go to the law firm. Is that correct?

Ms Hinchcliffe : On the search authorised on 22 August, the former secretary's and the former deputy secretary's emails were searched by DPS ICT. There were two other, more junior DPS employees whose data was extracted across those date ranges. For the extraction that occurred, that was authorised on 30 October, which was when TransPerfect extracted the mailboxes of the eight DPS employees for the date range that I have given. Then, yes, that included the former DPS secretary, former deputy secretary and other DPS employees.

Senator McGRATH: Did ICT give advice to you about concerns they have with either the searching or the release of information that could be covered by parliamentary privilege?

Ms Hinchcliffe : DPS ICT raised with me in their risk assessment the potential for material to be included that could be parliamentarian material or material to which parliamentary privilege applied.

Senator McGRATH: Shouldn't that have raised alarm bells?

Ms Hinchcliffe : In terms of the bulk extraction that occurred after the authorisation on 30 October, I went through a process of considering whether there were enough controls and protections in place to ensure that parliamentary privileged material did not go to the investigator, so could not be used as part of an investigation, and that it was then quarantined and kept safe in relation to TransPerfect holding that data.

Senator McGRATH: But, still, the IT department's division within DPS gave advice that the parliamentary privilege of parliamentarians could be breached by this, and yet DPS still made the decision to extract that information and release it to a third party?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I will be really clear about this. I made the decision. I considered the parliamentary privilege issue. I thought about that in terms of how I could ensure that your data as parliamentarians was protected, even though a bulk extraction was occurring, and how to ensure that no material that was parliamentarian material went to the investigator, which would be a breach of parliamentary privilege—

Senator McGRATH: With respect, Secretary, it did go to the law firm, a law firm who were hacked by the Russians, and it did go to their contractors.

Ms Hinchcliffe : It went to TransPerfect, who is a very well-respected legal data searching firm, and it went to TransPerfect after I had assurances in relation to the security of their system and the way that they would deal with that material, including the security of their systems, the security of their premises and how they would destroy the data once the investigation had been completed.

Senator McGRATH: Were all the decisions you made documented appropriately?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The decisions about providing access and authorisation for the searches to be made, yes.

Senator McGRATH: Can copies of that please be provided.

Ms Hinchcliffe : Yes, I'll take that on notice.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts.

Senator ROBERTS: President, thank you for your statement. I don't have any questions for you. My questions are mainly for Ms Hinchcliffe. Ms Hinchcliffe, what dates have you been employed at DPS or related agencies? My understanding is you were employed with DPS since 2015?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Yes, I think I started in April 2015 and was with the department until December 2017, when I was appointed the Deputy Commonwealth Ombudsman.

Senator ROBERTS: You were appointed Deputy Commonwealth Ombudsman?

Ms Hinchcliffe : That's right.

Senator ROBERTS: When did you leave that to go to the NACC?

Ms Hinchcliffe : No. I was then appointed the Integrity Commissioner of the Australian Commission of Law Enforcement Integrity.

Senator ROBERTS: What was that title?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The Integrity Commissioner of the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity—that was in February 2020. And then ACLEI, which is the acronym for that organisation, was mogged into the NACC on 1 July 2024.

Senator ROBERTS: What was your role at the NACC? Were you setting it up?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I was appointed by the then attorney as an acting deputy commissioner for a period during the initial months of the establishment of the NACC. Then I came to DPS as deputy secretary on, I think, 12 February last year. I think it was 12 February, because it was an estimates day.

Senator ROBERTS: You were here when Mr Stefanic's materials were raided, or taken, by the NACC?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I was here during the NACC search warrant, yes.

Senator ROBERTS: Did you hire Cate Saunders?

Ms Hinchcliffe : No.

Senator ROBERTS: What was your role in the DPS the first time? Was it HR manager, people and governance?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I think my title was assistant secretary—

Senator ROBERTS: HR?

Ms Hinchcliffe : governance and something. The HR team sat in my brief.

Senator ROBERTS: So you weren't involved even though you were overseeing HR?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Ms Saunders started after I left.

Senator ROBERTS: When did she start?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I think I provided evidence before to this committee on her start date. I don't know off the top of my head. We could find out for you.

Senator ROBERTS: If you could, please. Did you know Cate Saunders before she was hired?

Ms Hinchcliffe : No.

Senator ROBERTS: Not at all? Not working or professional—

Ms Hinchcliffe : No.

Senator ROBERTS: Coming to Fiona Roughley, was she employed as a research officer in the Senate?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I think she was employed as a research officer in the Senate. I think that is in her CV and on her website.

Senator ROBERTS: Did you know her before she was hired?

Ms Hinchcliffe : No.

Senator ROBERTS: You didn't have any idea of her?

Ms Hinchcliffe : No.

Senator ROBERTS: Who gave you a job as deputy secretary?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I went through a merit process, and there was an interview with an interview panel, and I was appointed through that process.

Senator ROBERTS: Who appointed you?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I assume that it was the then secretary.

Senator ROBERTS: You assume? There was no letter of offer?

Ms Hinchcliffe : You're absolutely right: I would have had a letter of offer. And, yes, it was signed by him. That would be the normal process.

Senator ROBERTS: That's Mr Stefanic?

Ms Hinchcliffe : That's right.

Senator ROBERTS: I'd like to come back and ask you questions about the department maintaining a suppression order in the case of ACD13. It hasn't been answered, so I'd like to ask it again. Why is the department maintaining the suppression order in the case of ACD13—a security officer—despite the complainant wanting it to be lifted?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The department is not a party to that suppression order and I have provided evidence to this committee before that it's not a matter that the department can make a decision on. That's a decision for the court. It's a matter for the court to decide. I think there is a provision in the suppression order that allows all parties to decide for the release of information, but the department is not a party to that.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you for that answer. My understanding—I'm not a lawyer and I'm not a judge—is that suppression orders are usually to protect the identity of the complainant. That complainant, ACD13, wants the suppression order lifted, so that doesn't really apply here. He doesn't need to protect his identity. The only reason left for the suppression order is for the protection of your own department from potential embarrassment. Is that correct?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I have already indicated this is not a matter for the department. We are not a party to those proceedings, so I can't do anything to lift the suppression order.

Senator ROBERTS: You can't take any notice of ACD13 wanting it lifted?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I can't do anything in relation to the suppression order.

The President: Senator Roberts, you have asked these questions before, and Ms Hinchcliffe has been clear the department is not a respondent in any way. There is nothing the department can do.

Senator ROBERTS: Okay, so I'll just recap, and I might cross paths, sometimes, with Senator McGrath. On 9 October, a DPS officer intercepted some mail to a politician in Parliament House, opened it and shared its contents with—

The President: Sorry, Senator Roberts, but you said, '9 October'. What year?

Senator ROBERTS: I've forgotten which year; I haven't got it.

The President: It's a bit hard to ask the officials about '9 October'. It could be 2018; it could be 2025.

Senator ROBERTS: With respect, President, the question will reveal itself. I think you'll know it, essentially, from my note.

CHAIR: I ask you to be cautious, Senator Roberts. I don't know what you're about to say, but in terms of staying within the bounds of—

Senator ROBERTS: Sure. This is a general overview. I'm checking to make sure I've got it correct. You've already pointed out one error in my checking. On 9 October in a year, a DPS officer intercepted some mail to a politician in Parliament House, opened it and shared its contents with at least two others over the period of 9 to 15 October of that year. Two decisions emerged: one, two days later, to allocate the June public interest disclosure for consideration and investigation; the other on 15 October to charge ACD13, a security officer, with the unauthorised disclosure of Commonwealth documents to a third party in breach of the parliamentary code of conduct and to impose restrictions on his work.

ACD13 identified the mail as his and attempted to make an external public interest disclosure, under whistleblower provisions, I think. Following on from the June public interest disclosure, ACD13 stopped working at DPS and was the complainant in the legal action. Are you confident you've implemented reforms to make sure senators communications and parliamentary privilege are absolutely protected?

The President: Senator Roberts, I can assist the committee. I am reliably informed that this was 2018. It was seven years ago. It absolutely predates Ms Hinchcliffe's employment, as she has demonstrated.

Senator ROBERTS: With respect, President, my question is: is Ms Hinchcliffe confident that she has implemented reforms to make sure senators communications and parliamentary privilege are absolutely protected?

Ms Hinchcliffe : In terms of the work that we are doing at the moment in our ICT area, and the discussion I'm having with Senator McGrath, that's quite different from my understanding of this case. Really, my understanding of this case comes from the Federal Court judgement rather than anything else about it. In this case, the Federal Court judgement has set out the reasons why they considered that no interim relief was required under the Public Interest Disclosure Act. Last time we discussed this at estimates, you raised with me a number of questions that went to issues that related to the understanding of the former secretary. After that, I sent you a letter that set out some evidence he had given in this matter at an estimates hearing previously. I'm not sure that I can add anything further in relation to this matter.

Senator ROBERTS: Did the person in ACD13's case who intercepted the mail addressed to a senator ever face any disciplinary action?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I don't have any further knowledge about this than what I've just provided you.

CHAIR: I would just point out that 2018 is not something I'd imagine Ms Hinchcliffe has a direct line of sight to in terms of what happened internally.

Senator ROBERTS: With regard to the bulk handover of material for the Roughley investigation, you've already answered that that was 'severe risk', or 'red'.

Ms Hinchcliffe : No, what I said was that I was provided with a draft risk assessment from the ICT team which I then discussed with them because of my concerns about it, as well as to give them the opportunity to raise their concerns about it, and we discussed a way forward. That draft risk assessment was never finalised. My understanding was that they were content with the procedure that we had come up with. That was my answer to Senator McGrath a moment ago.

Senator ROBERTS: This is my final question. Who is being held accountable for the data breach? Is it you, because you made the final decision?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Which data breach?

Senator ROBERTS: The original data breach—ACD13's case. Oh, sorry, you weren't involved.

Ms Hinchcliffe : I wasn't involved in that. I've just received some further information. You asked a question about when Ms Saunders started with the department. It was 7 December 2017.

Senator ROBERTS: Okay. Thank you.

CHAIR: We just need to be cautious about conflating different issues in this context, Senator Roberts.

Senator HUME: I have a couple of clarification questions. The first is about the risk assessment. Ms Hinchcliffe, you said the terminology was red, green and yellow. Was it just colours, or were there words attached to it? Was it low, medium, high, moderate?

Ms Hinchcliffe : There were words attached to it.

Senator HUME: What were the words that were associated with red?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I think the words usually associated with it are 'severe' and 'extreme', but I can check that for you.

Senator HUME: Severe and extreme risk?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Yes. It was a red risk.

Senator HUME: So that was the draft risk assessment.

Ms Hinchcliffe : That's right.

Senator HUME: You said you felt that you had worked through the issues pointed out in that draft assessment and then proceeded.

Ms Hinchcliffe : Then the DPS ICT team proceeded with undertaking the bulk extraction in relation to two DPS employees and conducted searches in relation to the other six DPS employees.

Senator HUME: Does the ICT team usually proceed with a task that requires a risk assessment without that risk assessment not being in draft form?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I don't know the answer to that. That was what occurred on this occasion.

Senator HUME: Did anyone in the ICT division request a risk assessment that wasn't in draft form?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Not that I'm aware of. I only received the draft risk assessment. Then I had the discussion with the former chief information officer. We came to an agreement about how we would proceed. I was not provided with a further draft assessment. My understanding was that that had allayed any concerns and that there was no further need.

Senator HUME: Just for the sake of a paper trail, for your own security, surely you would have wanted to have had a formal and final risk assessment upon which you have clearly responded, reacted, acted and directed?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I was not provided with a final risk assessment.

Senator HUME: What are the options given to you on the way to respond to a draft risk assessment? Does it say 'go, stop, discuss, consider'? What do you have to do?

Ms Hinchcliffe : The draft is marked as a draft. It was provided to me as a draft for discussion. We had a meeting the next day and we discussed and resolved a way forward.

Senator HUME: Did you ask for a risk assessment before you proceeded?

Ms Hinchcliffe : No, I did not.

Senator HUME: Why not?

Ms Hinchcliffe : Because, in relation to the provision of the authorisation on 22 August—sorry, I don't want to confuse the dates, given there were three different authorisations that were given. I provided that authorisation and I included in that email correspondence that I was happy to discuss if the former chief information officer would like to discuss a different way forward. Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you for your time this evening, Secretary. I'm keen to ask a few things about the department's policy on bullying and then come back to some ICT questions. The secretary and the executive team are very focused on making sure that we are providing a workplace that is free of bullying and harassment and that staff feel safe and supported to be able to come to work. There are processes that our staff can go through to be able to report instances of bullying, harassment or other inappropriate behaviour. That will depend on how that information is assessed as to what the next steps are. If, for instance, it is something that is serious and constitutes serious bullying and harassment, there are options that the department can go through in terms of internal investigation, external investigation and consideration against whether the actions have or haven't impacted the Parliamentary Service Code of Conduct and also the Parliamentary Service Values. If it is something which is more anecdotal and cannot be verified, conversations can be had with individuals and with teams. Obviously, those conversations are also documented when it's appropriate to do so.

All government departments that I've ever had the privilege of being able to work in have got circumstances where staff have felt unsatisfied, though, with the results of an investigation that's occurred. For me, as someone who's been involved in HR for a period of time, that's a really challenging situation to be able to work through, because obviously you may have taken all of the appropriate steps to be able to identify, rectify and call out and to put in place management arrangements for the person against whom the allegation has been made, but it is also not appropriate, at times, to go back to the person who made the allegation to be able to give them the specifics of what has actually occurred. Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you.

We never want to see a situation where we have zero reports of bullying and harassment, because that also can indicate a culture of people not wanting to report. We want to have a culture where inappropriate behaviour is called out, action is taken, people are challenged on the actions and behaviours that they have experienced and constructive conversations are held with people against whom concerns have been raised but we also give our staff the confidence of knowing that we do actually take action when it's called out.

Ms Hinder : We have very well-publicised methods of how to be able to do that. The department has an employee assistance provider, TELUS Health. Senator WHITEAKER: Thanks, all, for coming back to us again today. I have a couple of questions relating to First Nations employees, if you're able to assist. Can you outline what resources are available to First Nations staff within DPS to support and promote their careers?

Ms Hinchcliffe : I'll ask Mr Lucas to come forward to answer your question.

Mr Lucas : The department has worked closely with colleagues across the parliamentary service, and it's assisted by the Parliamentary Services Indigenous Employee Network to support First Nations staff with their parliamentary careers. In terms of resources, we have an inclusion and pathway team, which are available to discuss and provide guidance to our First Nations staff and to support managers in their role in fostering our First Nations staff. First Nations staff are also able to reach into the Parliamentary Services Indigenous Employee Network, PSIEN. That's an APH-wide network dedicated to supporting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander staff. That's open to all First Nations employees across parliamentary departments.

In terms of additional broad supports afforded to employees and in recognition that employees may wish to celebrate and participate in culturally significant days and events which are not prescribed public holidays, they may access additional paid leave. They are able to access an additional one day of paid leave per calendar year to participate in NAIDOC Week activities. And the department, delightfully, also participates in the Australian Government Indigenous Apprenticeships Program. That's an initiative designed to enhance employment opportunities for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples throughout the APS.

Senator WHITEAKER: How are DPS fostering a workplace environment that helps First Nations staff progress into leadership positions?

Mr Lucas : In addition to a lot of the supports we put around that I just noted, we have put in place substantive effort into training and development. All our staff through DPS are required to complete the core cultural awareness training within the first three months of their employment within the department.
